title: Project management planning
exam_coverage_note: 11 of 60 marks. The largest objective in the syllabus, worth almost a fifth of the paper.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 1.2.2, 1.2.3, 1.3.5, 1.3.7, 2.3, 3.1, 4.1.1, 4.2, 4.2.4, 4.2.10, 4.3, 4.3.1 and 8th ed. 2.4, 3.1.3, 3.6, 4.1, 5.1.1, 5.4, 5.4.1, 5.5.3, 5.5.4.

where_this_fits: Eleven marks, more than any other objective and nearly a fifth of the paper. If your study time is limited, this is where it goes. The objective covers what gets a project from an idea to an agreed plan: the business case that justifies it, the baseline that measures it, the estimates that size it, the stakeholder analysis that keeps people on side, the success criteria that define done, and the reporting that shows whether it is working.

key_definitions.definition: The approved plan against which project progress is measured and controlled.
key_definitions.plain_english: The agreed version of the plan. Everything you report afterwards is measured against it.

key_definitions.definition: The document setting out why, what, how, when, how much and by whom a project will be delivered, produced by the project manager and approved by the sponsor.
key_definitions.plain_english: The single document that says how this project will actually be run.

key_definitions.definition: The document providing justification for undertaking a project, setting out costs, benefits, risks, options and timescales.
key_definitions.plain_english: The answer to why should we do this, and is it still worth doing.

key_definitions.definition: The identification and assessment of stakeholders' interest in and influence over a project, used to plan engagement.
key_definitions.plain_english: Working out who cares, who can affect the outcome, and how to deal with each of them.

key_definitions.definition: The identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of business benefits.
key_definitions.plain_english: Making sure the improvement the project was funded to produce actually turns up.

key_definitions.definition: A representation of how estimating accuracy improves through the life cycle as uncertainty reduces.
key_definitions.plain_english: Early estimates are wide guesses. Later ones are narrow. The funnel is that shape drawn out.

key_definitions.definition: The measures by which the success of a project is judged.
key_definitions.plain_english: What has to be true at the end for everyone to agree it went well.

core_content.key_takeaway: A deployment baseline is the approved plan that project progress is measured and controlled against. It normally covers scope, schedule and cost together, and is set once that plan is approved. Baseline means reference point, not start date.
core_content.body_markdown:
The word to hold on to is reference.

Once the plan is baselined, anyone can ask a precise question: are we ahead or behind, over or under, against what we agreed? Without a baseline that question has no answer, because there is nothing to compare against.

A baseline normally covers scope, schedule and cost together. Changing any of them changes what the project is being measured against, which is why changes have to go through a formal process. You cannot quietly move a baseline, because moving it makes every earlier progress report meaningless.

In a linear life cycle, baselining happens at the end of the definition phase, once scope, schedule and cost are settled and approved.

core_content.outcome_title: State how deployment baselines differ between linear and iterative life cycles
core_content.key_takeaway: In a linear life cycle the deployment baseline is set once, for the whole project, at the end of definition, and changing it needs formal change control. In an iterative life cycle a baseline is set for each iteration in turn, with the detail of later iterations deliberately left open.
core_content.body_markdown:
The difference follows from what each life cycle fixes.

Linear fixes scope, and flexes time and cost through change control. So the whole project can be measured against one agreed plan, set at the end of definition.

Iterative fixes time and cost for each iteration, and flexes scope by re-prioritising what goes into it. So the baseline is set iteration by iteration.

There is still a high level plan for an iterative project as a whole. What is baselined in detail is only the current cycle.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the stakeholders of a project management plan
core_content.key_takeaway: The stakeholders of a project management plan are the people with an interest in it: the sponsor, who approves it, the project manager, who produces it and works to it, team members, who find their work packages in it, suppliers, whose commitments depend on it, end users, who learn what they will receive and when, and the governance board, which uses it to set tolerances and take decisions. Being a stakeholder means having an interest in the plan, not having written it.
core_content.body_markdown:
The project management plan sets out why, what, how, when, how much and by whom the project will be delivered. Several groups have a stake in it, each for a different reason.

The sponsor approves the plan and owns the business case it serves. Their interest is whether the plan will deliver the benefits they are accountable for.

The project manager produces the plan and works to it. It is the document they are held to.

Project team members find their own work in it, as work packages, schedules and responsibilities.

Suppliers are stakeholders because the plan states what will be bought and when it is needed.

End users have a stake because the plan decides what they will receive and when, and what will be expected of them at handover.

The governance board uses the plan as the basis for the tolerances it sets and the decisions it takes.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the purpose and typical content of a business case
core_content.key_takeaway: The business case provides the justification for undertaking the project, and keeps answering whether it is still worth doing. Typical content is the strategic reason, the options considered including do nothing, the expected costs, the expected benefits, the major risks and the timescales. It is reviewed at each decision gate rather than written once.
core_content.body_markdown:
The business case answers one question and keeps answering it: is this still worth doing?

A do nothing option is normally among the options considered, because it sets the baseline the others are judged against.

The business case is not a delivery document. Work breakdown structures, detailed schedules and issue logs belong elsewhere. If an option in a question describes something a project manager would use to run the work, it is not business case content.

The business case is live rather than one off. It is created at concept, approved before the project proceeds, and reviewed at each decision gate. A project whose costs have doubled and whose benefits have halved should fail its next gate, and the business case is how that becomes visible.

core_content.outcome_title: Explain the role of the project sponsor and project manager in relation to developing a business case
core_content.key_takeaway: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for developing and maintaining it through the life of the project. The project manager supplies the information that keeps it accurate, such as cost forecasts, schedule position and changes in risk. The project manager does not own it and does not approve it.
core_content.body_markdown:
When a decision gate asks whether the project should continue, it is the sponsor's business case that answers.

The project manager gives the sponsor what they need to answer it: current cost forecasts, schedule position, changes in risk, anything that alters the picture.

The split matters because the two roles can pull in opposite directions. A project manager measured on delivery has an incentive to keep delivering. A sponsor accountable for benefits has an incentive to stop a project that no longer justifies its cost. Separating ownership of the business case from responsibility for delivery is what makes it possible to cancel a project that is being run well but is no longer worth doing.

core_content.outcome_title: Explain how stakeholder analysis supports effective stakeholder engagement
core_content.key_takeaway: Stakeholder analysis identifies who has an interest in the project and how much influence they have over it, usually by assessing each stakeholder on those two axes. Engagement is then targeted: manage high influence and high interest closely, keep high influence and low interest satisfied, keep high interest and low influence informed, and monitor the rest. It directs finite effort where it changes the outcome, and does not guarantee support.
core_content.body_markdown:
Stakeholder analysis identifies who has an interest in the project and how much influence they have over it. Engagement is then planned accordingly.

The usual approach places each stakeholder on two axes, interest and influence, and treats them differently depending on where they land.

| Position | Approach |
|---|---|
| High influence, high interest | Manage closely |
| High influence, low interest | Keep satisfied |
| Low influence, high interest | Keep informed |
| Low influence, low interest | Monitor |

The value is in the targeting. Engagement effort is limited, and spreading it evenly means the people who could sink the project get the same attention as the people who could not. Analysis is what lets you spend the effort where it changes the outcome.

What comes out of the analysis then shapes the communication plan: who gets what information, when, and how.

core_content.key_takeaway: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of business benefits. A benefit is the measurable improvement that follows when an output is used, so a benefit is not the same thing as an output. The project manager is accountable for outputs and the sponsor is accountable for benefits.
core_content.body_markdown:
The distinction the exam cares about is benefits against outputs.

A project delivers outputs: the new system, the finished building, the trained staff. Benefits are the measurable improvement that follows when those outputs get used. A new system nobody logs into has been delivered and has produced no benefit at all.

That is why benefits management carries on past the end of delivery, and why accountability splits the way it does.

Benefits are identified in the business case, planned during definition, tracked through delivery, and confirmed at a benefits review after handover.

core_content.key_takeaway: The three estimating methods are analytical, analogous and parametric. Analytical, also called bottom up, breaks the work into small components, estimates each one and adds them up. Analogous uses actual data from similar past work and adjusts it, and parametric uses a measured rate such as cost per square metre or hours per test case.
core_content.body_markdown:
The three methods suit different points in a project.

Analytical estimating is the most accurate and the most expensive to produce, because the work has to be understood in detail first.

Analogous estimating is quick and cheap. It depends entirely on having comparable history, and on the honesty of the adjustment made for the differences.

Parametric estimating is reliable where the measured relationship genuinely holds, and misleading where it does not.

Analogous and parametric estimates are what you can produce early, when little is known. Analytical estimates become possible later, once the work is defined.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the purpose of the estimating funnel
core_content.key_takeaway: The estimating funnel shows how the accuracy of estimates improves as the project progresses and uncertainty falls. The range around an estimate is very wide at concept and narrows as assumptions are replaced by facts. It is about accuracy, not about cost.
core_content.body_markdown:
At concept, almost nothing is known and the range around any estimate is very wide. As the project moves through definition and into delivery, more becomes known, assumptions are replaced by facts, and the range narrows. Drawn as a shape, that range starts wide and closes, which is why it is called a funnel.

The practical use is managing expectations. A sponsor asking for a number at concept should be given a range, and told why it is a range. Presenting an early estimate as a single confident figure is how projects end up with budgets they were never going to meet.

The funnel also explains why estimates should be revisited at each phase rather than produced once. An estimate is a statement about what was known at the time it was made.

core_content.outcome_title: Explain why establishing success criteria is important at the start, during, and at the handover of a project
core_content.key_takeaway: Success criteria are the measures by which the success of the project is judged. At the start they define what everyone is aiming at, during the project they give changes and trade-offs a reference point, and at handover they are the basis for judging whether the project succeeded. Agreeing them at the start removes the argument at the end.
core_content.body_markdown:
The outcome names three points in time, and each has its own reason.

At the start, success criteria force disagreement into the open while it is still cheap to resolve. Without them, different stakeholders carry different definitions of success all the way to handover and only discover it there.

During the project, they give decisions a reference. When a change is proposed or a trade-off is forced, the question becomes whether it moves the project towards or away from the agreed criteria. Without them, trade-offs get settled by whoever is loudest.

At handover, they are what acceptance is measured against, rather than expectations that formed along the way.

Success criteria are about the project as a whole. They are not the same as acceptance criteria, which say whether one specific deliverable is fit for purpose.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the purpose and benefits of project progress reporting
core_content.key_takeaway: Progress reporting communicates the project's position against its baseline: what is complete, what it has cost, what remains and what has changed. Its purpose is to make variance visible early enough for someone to act on it. The benefits are timely and consistent information for stakeholders, evidence for the sponsor and the governance board, and a record of what was known when.
core_content.body_markdown:
The purpose is to enable decisions.

A variance spotted early can be corrected cheaply. The same variance discovered at handover cannot be corrected at all. Reporting exists to shorten the gap between something going wrong and somebody being able to do something about it.

The benefits are worth being able to state. Stakeholders get timely, consistent information instead of rumour. The sponsor gets what they need to judge whether the business case still holds. The governance board gets the evidence it needs to make decisions. Problems surface while they are still small. And the project keeps a record of what was known when.

Reporting needs an approved baseline to report against. Without one, progress reporting turns into describing activity rather than measuring performance.

misconceptions.wrong: A baseline is the date the project starts.
misconceptions.right: A baseline is the approved plan that progress is measured against. It covers scope, schedule and cost, and changing it requires change control.
They baseline each iteration rather than the whole project at once.

misconceptions.wrong: The project manager owns the business case.
misconceptions.right: The sponsor owns it. The project manager supplies the information that keeps it accurate.

misconceptions.wrong: The business case is written once, at the start.
misconceptions.right: It is maintained throughout and reviewed at every decision gate. Its job is to keep answering whether the project is still worth doing.

misconceptions.wrong: Benefits and outputs are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Outputs are what the project delivers. Benefits are the measurable improvement that follows when someone uses them. An unused output produces no benefit.

misconceptions.wrong: The estimating funnel shows costs falling as the project progresses.
misconceptions.right: It shows estimating accuracy improving as uncertainty reduces. Costs may do anything.

misconceptions.wrong: Analytical estimating is always the right choice because it is the most accurate.
misconceptions.right: It requires the work to be understood in detail first, so it is unavailable early. Analogous and parametric methods exist because a number is needed before that point.
It tells you who matters and how, so engagement can be targeted. Some stakeholders will oppose the project no matter how well they are analysed.

misconceptions.wrong: Progress reporting keeps the project on track.
misconceptions.right: It makes deviation visible early enough for someone to act. The acting is a separate thing.

memory_aids.expansion: Analytical, Analogous, Parametric. The three estimating methods named in the syllabus. Anything else in a list is a distractor.
The project delivers the output. The benefit arrives when someone uses it. Project manager owns the first, sponsor owns the second.
Sponsor owns the business case. Project manager informs it. Same why-versus-how split as objective 3.
If a question is about progress, variance or control, the answer almost always involves the baseline.
The estimating funnel in three words. Accuracy improves; it says nothing about whether costs go up or down.

progress_checkpoint: I can define a deployment baseline without using the word start, and say how baselines differ between linear and iterative life cycles.
I can name four stakeholders of the project management plan with a reason for each, and say who owns the business case and who informs it.
I can list the typical contents of a business case and name two things that do not belong in it.
I can explain what stakeholder analysis produces and what it cannot promise.
I can define benefits management and explain the difference between a benefit and an output.
I can name the three estimating methods, say what the estimating funnel shows, and give three benefits of progress reporting.
